questions.q: cart = ["Masala Box", "Cotton Kurta", "Steel Water Bottle"]. What is cart[1]?
questions.explain: Positions start at 0, so cart[0] is Masala Box and cart[1] is the second item. cart[-1] would be the last one.

questions.q: Which container fits ONE Bazaar product with a name, a price and a seller?
questions.explain: Each value has a meaning, so look it up by name: product["seller"] is clearer than product[2].

questions.q: product has no "rating" key. What does product.get("rating") give?
questions.explain: .get gives None (or the default you pass) for a missing key. product["rating"] would crash with a KeyError.

questions.q: You add "Sharma Electronics" twice to a set of sellers. How many times is it in the set?
questions.explain: A set keeps each value once. That's why 5 seller names with one repeat give 4 sellers.

questions.q: same_cart = ashas_cart, then same_cart.append("Cotton Kurta"). What does ashas_cart contain?
options: Its old items plus Cotton Kurta: both names point to the same list
questions.explain: = never copies. Lists can change, so a change through one name is seen through the other. Use ashas_cart.copy() for a separate list.

questions.q: line = ("Masala Box", 29900, 2). What does line[2] = 3 do?
options: TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
questions.explain: Tuples can't be changed. Make a new tuple, or use a list if the values must change.

questions.q: (Going deeper) Why is "Patel Spices" in sellers fast even with millions of sellers, when sellers is a set?
options: Sets use a hash table: the value's hash tells Python almost exactly where to look
It isn't faster than a list
questions.explain: A list checks items one by one; a set or dict jumps straight to the right place. That's also why their items must be hashable (not lists).

questions.q: (Going deeper) catalog is a list of dicts. shallow = catalog.copy(); shallow[0]["stock"] = 2. Does catalog change?
options: Yes: .copy() is shallow, so the inner dicts are shared; copy.deepcopy() copies them too
questions.explain: A shallow copy makes a new outer list holding the SAME product dicts. Changing a product through either list changes it for both.
